Worse
WURS
adj., adv.
Comparative of bad or ill, from Old English wyrsa. Webster 1828: more bad, or more evil; less good. In the Authorized Version it is chiefly the historians’ verdict on successive generations, and the New Testament’s verdict on apostasy and on neglect of one’s own household.

Biblical Definition

Worse is the word Scripture uses when a generation has taken what it received and made it lower. Omri wrought evil in the eyes of the LORD, and did worse than all that were before him (1 Kings 16:25). Manasseh made Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem to err, and to do worse than the heathen, whom the LORD had destroyed before the children of Israel (2 Chronicles 33:9) — the covenant nation outdoing the nations it had displaced. Jeremiah says it twice of his own contemporaries: they did worse than their fathers (Jeremiah 7:26), and ye have done worse than your fathers (Jeremiah 16:12). Decline is not automatic in Scripture, but it is common, and the prophets treat each generation as responsible for it. The New Testament sharpens the word. Peter says of those who escape the world’s pollutions through knowledge of Christ and are entangled again, the latter end is worse with them than the beginning (2 Peter 2:20). Paul says that a man who provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house… is worse than an infidel (1 Timothy 5:8). And Paul rebukes a church whose gatherings had begun to harm it: ye come together not for the better, but for the worse (1 Corinthians 11:17).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines WORSE as more bad or more evil; less good; and, of health, more sick. It is the comparative of ill, and the KJV uses it as a moral and covenantal verdict rather than a mere measure of degree.

expand to see more

WORSE, a. — More bad or more evil; less good; inferior in goodness or quality.

In a state of health, more sick; as, the patient is worse.

WORSE, adv. — In a manner more evil or bad; as, they did worse than their fathers.

Webster’s adverbial illustration is itself a paraphrase of Jeremiah, which shows how thoroughly the biblical idiom had entered the English of his day.

Key Scripture

1 Kings 16:25 — "But Omri wrought evil in the eyes of the LORD, and did worse than all that were before him."

2 Chronicles 33:9 — "So Manasseh made Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem to err, and to do worse than the heathen, whom the LORD had destroyed before the children of Israel."

Jeremiah 16:12 — "And ye have done worse than your fathers; for, behold, ye walk every one after the imagination of his evil heart, that they may not hearken unto me:"

2 Peter 2:20 — "For if after they have escaped the pollutions of the world through the knowledge of the Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, they are again entangled therein, and overcome, the latter end is worse with them than the beginning."

1 Timothy 5:8 — "But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel."

Modern Corruption

The word is corrupted by the modern assumption of progress — that later is by definition better — and by the therapeutic instinct that will not permit a comparative moral verdict on a generation, a church, or a man at all.

expand to see more

Scripture’s historians are perfectly willing to say that a generation is worse than the one before it, and to name the men responsible. Jeremiah 16:12 does not hedge: ye have done worse than your fathers, and the reason given is that each man walks after the imagination of his evil heart. The reigning assumption of the last two centuries is the reverse — that the arc of history bends upward and that later opinion is by that fact more enlightened. Where that assumption governs, 2 Chronicles 33:9 becomes unreadable, because it says a covenant people can sink below the pagans they replaced. The Chronicler’s verdicts are this dictionary’s verdicts. Faithful kings are named faithful; apostate kings are named apostate; and generations are measured against the light they were given.

1 Timothy 5:8 and 2 Peter 2:20 are the two comparatives that fall on individuals, and both are severe. A man who will not provide for his own household is worse than an infidel — worse, that is, than a man who makes no Christian profession at all, because the unbeliever generally still feeds his children. And the apostate who has known the way of righteousness and turned from it is in a worse state than before he knew it. Neither verse can be softened into a comment on someone’s difficulties. They are the New Testament’s warning that light received raises the stakes, and that a profession abandoned leaves a man lower than where it found him.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Hebrew idiom is to do evil more than those before; the Greek uses ordinary comparatives of bad and worse. The English comparative renders both without a distinct lemma of its own.

expand to see more

Hebrew ra'a' (H7489) — to be evil, to do wickedly; the comparative is formed with min, more than (1 Kings 16:25; Jeremiah 16:12).

Greek cheiron (G5501) — worse; the latter end is worse with them than the beginning (2 Peter 2:20) and the rent is made worse (Matthew 9:16).

Greek apistos (G571) — unbelieving, an infidel; the standard against which the neglectful provider is measured (1 Timothy 5:8).

Greek hesson (G2276) — less, worse; not for the better, but for the worse (1 Corinthians 11:17).

The Chronicler’s comparative verdicts on the kings are a fixed literary device, not a rhetorical exaggeration.

Usage

"Did worse than all that were before him (1 Kings 16:25) — the historian’s verdict on a king, stated plainly."

"The latter end is worse with them than the beginning (2 Peter 2:20) — apostasy leaves a man lower than it found him."

"Worse than an infidel (1 Timothy 5:8) — the provider who neglects his own house measured against a man with no profession at all."
